deep.reconstruction: There is no mathematics on this page. It is a page of German notes on ancient Persian history, in the style of a lecture or textbook summary (Achaemenid succession, 424-404 BC). It continues the previous page (Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I Longimanus, the Peace of Callias 449) and leads into the next page (Cyrus the Younger, the Ten Thousand, Cunaxa 401). Content in order: (1) Artaxerxes I dies in 424 and leaves one legitimate son, Xerxes II. After 45 days Xerxes II is overthrown by his illegitimate brother Sogdianus. (2) Sogdianus lasts only a few months and is overthrown in 423 by another illegitimate brother, Ochus, who takes the name Darius II and rules until 404. (3) Darius II is called a weak ruler. Like his predecessors he faced internal revolts, which could only be dealt with by money/cunning; the wording is uncertain. (4) The Persian empire survived only because the Greeks were fighting each other (the Peloponnesian War). (5) In Asia Minor ('Vorderasien') the satrap Tissaphernes, 'the slyest of governors', kept playing Athens and Sparta against each other. (6) In Darius II's last years his younger son Cyrus was sent to Asia Minor and openly sided with Sparta. (7) Darius dies in 404, leaving two sons, Cyrus and Artaxerxes. Artaxerxes takes the throne with the epithet Mnemon. He is described as good-natured, with many virtues that (continuing on the next page) made him an excellent private man but not a ruler. No derivation, computation or mathematical problem is present. The hand and subject suggest school or lecture notes filed in the Gauss papers, possibly not by Gauss himself (unsure).
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. The historical content broadly agrees with the standard account (Ctesias/Diodorus): Xerxes II reigned about 45 days, Sogdianus about 6 months, Darius II 423-404, and Cyrus the Younger was sent west around 408/407 and backed Sparta. 'Darius left 2 sons' simplifies things: Darius II had further sons, e.g. Ostanes and Oxathres, but Cyrus and Artaxerxes were the relevant ones.

results.what: Narrative of the Achaemenid succession 424-404 BC and Persian policy toward Athens and Sparta (Tissaphernes, Cyrus the Younger)
results.modern_name: Ancient history notes (Achaemenid Persia, late 5th century BC); not mathematics
results.usually_credited_to: Standard classical sources (Thucydides, Xenophon, Ctesias, Diodorus) as transmitted in 18th/19th-century history textbooks

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains only routine school or lecture history notes on Persian kings, with no mathematical content. It is possibly not even in Gauss's hand. Nothing here would interest a historian of mathematics beyond the archival curiosity of its being filed in the bundle.
transcription_corrections: Last line: 'hatte viele Ehegatten[?], die ihn zum besten führt[?]' should read 'hatte viele Tugenden, die ihn zum besten Privat[mann]...'. The next page starts with 'mann, aber nicht zum Fürsten machten', giving the standard characterization of Artaxerxes II as a good private man but a poor ruler.

Line 9-10: 'und man konnte sich nur durch[?] und List retten[?]' is uncertain. The final word looks more like 'entledigen' (rid oneself of) than 'retten'. The phrase is plausibly 'durch Gold/Geld und List entledigen'.
Line 14: 'Kriegsheer[?] zu unterhalten' is doubtful. The word appears shorter, possibly 'Ansehen' or similar; it remains uncertain.
Line 14: 'In {+V+}order{+a+}sien' is correct as 'In Vorderasien', with superscript insertions visible in the image.
